cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: How are you getting on with your art project, Tom?

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: OK. Like, they gave us the theme of birds to base our project on, and I’m not really all that interested in wildlife. But I’m starting to get into it. I’ve pretty well finished the introductory stage.

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: So have I. When they gave us all those handouts with details of books and websites to look at (Q21/Q22), I was really put off, but the more I read, the more interested I got.

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: Me too. I found I could research so many different aspects of birds in art – colour, movement, texture. So I was looking forward to the Bird Park visit.

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: What a letdown! It poured with rain and we hardly saw a single bird. Much less use than the trip to the Natural History Museum (Q21/Q22).

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: Yeah, I liked all the stuff about evolution there. The workshop sessions with Dr Fletcher were good too, especially the brainstorming sessions.

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: I missed those because I was ill. I wish we could’ve seen the projects last year’s students did.

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: Mm. I suppose they want us to do our own thing, not copy.

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: Have you drafted your proposal yet?

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: Yes, but I haven’t handed it in. I need to amend some parts. I’ve realised the notes from my research are almost all just descriptions, I haven’t actually evaluated anything. So I’ll have to fix that (Q23/Q24).

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: Oh, I didn’t know we had to do that. I’ll have to look at that too. Did you do a timeline for the project?

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: Yes, and a mind map.

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: Yeah, so did I. I quite enjoyed that. But it was hard having to explain the basis for my decisions in my action plan.

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: What?

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: You know, give a rationale.

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: I didn’t realise we had to do that. OK, I can add it now. And I’ve done the video diary presentation, and worked out what I want my outcome to be in the project.

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: Someone told me it’s best not to be too precise about your actual outcome (Q23/Q24) at this stage, so you have more scope to explore your ideas later on. So I’m going to go back to my proposal to make it a bit more vague.

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: Really? OK, I’ll change that too then.

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: One part of the project I’m unsure about is where we choose some paintings of birds and say what they mean to us. Like, I chose a painting of a falcon by Landseer. I like it because the bird’s standing there with his head turned to one side, but he seems to be staring straight at you. But I can’t just say it’s a bit scary, can I?

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: You could talk about the possible danger suggested by the bird’s look (Q25).

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: Oh, OK.

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: There’s a picture of a fish hawk by Audubon I like. It’s swooping over the water with a fish in its talons, and with great black wings which take up most of the picture.

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: So you could discuss it in relation to predators and food chains?

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: Well actually I think I’ll concentrate on the impression of rapid motion it gives. (Q26)

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: Right.

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: Do you know that picture of a kingfisher by van Gogh – it’s perching on a reed growing near a stream.

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: Yes, it’s got these beautiful blue and red and black shades.

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: Mm hm. I’ve actually chosen it because I saw a real kingfisher once when I was little, I was out walking with my grandfather (Q27), and I’ve never forgotten it.

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: So we can use a personal link?

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: Sure.

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: OK. There’s a portrait called William Wells. I can’t remember the artist but it’s a middle-aged man who’s just shot a bird. And his expression, and the way he’s holding the bird in his hand suggests he’s not sure about what he’s done. To me it’s about how ambiguous people are in the way they exploit the natural world. (Q28)

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: Interesting. There’s Gauguin’s picture Vairumati. He did it in Tahiti. It’s a woman with a white bird behind her that is eating a lizard, and what I’m interested in is what idea this bird refers to. Apparently, it’s a reference to the never-ending cycle of existence. (Q29)

cues.speaker: TOM
cues.text: Wow. I chose a portrait of a little boy, Giovanni de Medici. He’s holding a tiny bird in one fist (Q30). I like the way he’s holding it carefully so he doesn’t hurt it.

cues.speaker: JESS
cues.text: Ah right.
